canon.title: Achievement of Target Gain Larger than Unity in an Inertial Fusion Experiment
canon.why: 2.05 MJ of laser light in, 3.1 MJ of fusion out. Seventy years of trying, finally over the line.

canon.title: Highly accurate protein structure prediction with AlphaFold
canon.why: A fifty-year-old problem, largely solved. The structures are free for every known protein.

canon.title: Language Models are Few-Shot Learners
canon.why: GPT-3. The paper where scaling alone started producing abilities nobody trained for.

canon.title: Attention Is All You Need
canon.why: The transformer. Every large language model in use today is a descendant of this one paper.

canon.title: Observation of Gravitational Waves from a Binary Black Hole Merger
canon.why: Spacetime itself was measured ringing, a century after Einstein said it would.

canon.title: Deep Residual Learning for Image Recognition
canon.why: Skip connections made very deep networks trainable. Almost everything since is built on them.

canon.title: Generative Adversarial Networks
canon.why: Two networks trained against each other — the idea that made generated images convincing.

canon.title: Observation of a new particle in the search for the Standard Model Higgs boson
canon.why: The last missing piece of the Standard Model, found 48 years after it was predicted.

canon.title: A Programmable Dual-RNA–Guided DNA Endonuclease in Adaptive Bacterial Immunity
canon.who: Jinek, Chylinski, Fonfara, Hauer, Doudna and Charpentier
canon.why: CRISPR-Cas9 turned from a bacterial immune system into a tool for editing any genome.

canon.title: Suppression of RNA Recognition by Toll-like Receptors
canon.why: The modified-nucleoside trick that stops the body attacking mRNA. Ignored for years, then it made the COVID vaccines work.

canon.title: Observational Evidence from Supernovae for an Accelerating Universe
canon.why: The expansion is speeding up, and nobody knows why. Dark energy is the name for not knowing.

canon.title: Evidence for Oscillation of Atmospheric Neutrinos
canon.why: Neutrinos change type as they travel, which means they have mass — the Standard Model said they did not.

canon.title: LixCoO2: A new cathode material for batteries of high energy density
canon.why: The cathode inside the lithium-ion battery in your phone. A Nobel, 39 years later.

canon.title: The hippocampus as a spatial map
canon.why: The discovery of place cells — the brain's internal map. Nobel Prize 2014.

canon.title: Self-Consistent Equations Including Exchange and Correlation Effects
canon.why: The practical form of density functional theory — how most of computational chemistry works today.

canon.title: A Measurement of Excess Antenna Temperature at 4080 Mc/s
canon.why: They thought it was pigeon droppings in the antenna. It was the afterglow of the Big Bang.

canon.title: Receptive fields, binocular interaction and functional architecture in the cat's visual cortex
canon.why: How the visual cortex builds edges and shapes out of spots of light — and an inspiration for convolutional networks.

canon.title: Detailed Balance Limit of Efficiency of p-n Junction Solar Cells
canon.why: Why a single solar cell tops out near a third of the sunlight it catches — and why tandems exist.

canon.title: Experimental Test of Parity Conservation in Beta Decay
canon.why: Nature tells left from right. Physicists had assumed for decades that it could not.

canon.title: Synthesis of the Elements in Stars
canon.why: How every element heavier than helium got made. The paper that ties nuclear physics to the sky.

canon.title: Some Criteria for a Power Producing Thermonuclear Reactor
canon.why: How hot, how dense and for how long — the bar every fusion machine is still measured against.

canon.title: Molecular Structure of Nucleic Acids: A Structure for Deoxyribose Nucleic Acid
canon.why: One page, and the double helix. Built on Rosalind Franklin's X-ray data, which she was not told they had.

canon.title: A quantitative description of membrane current and its application to conduction and excitation in nerve
canon.why: The equations for how a neuron fires. Still the basis of every realistic neuron model.

canon.title: Über den Nachweis und das Verhalten der bei der Bestrahlung des Urans mittels Neutronen entstehenden Erdalkalimetalle
canon.why: The chemistry showing uranium had split into barium. They could not explain it, and published anyway.

canon.title: Disintegration of Uranium by Neutrons: a New Type of Nuclear Reaction
canon.why: The explanation Hahn could not give, worked out over a winter walk. Meitner was left off the Nobel.

canon.title: The Nature of the Chemical Bond
canon.why: Quantum mechanics turned into the chemist's everyday picture of bonds and hybrid orbitals.

canon.title: A relation between distance and radial velocity among extra-galactic nebulae
canon.why: Two and a half pages showing the universe is expanding. Cosmology starts here.

items.title: A spatial map of the atmospheric limb of a hot Jupiter
items.license: Crossref metadata CC0; abstract as deposited by publisher
items.abstract: Planets are inherently three-dimensional objects shaped by their thermal structure and dynamics. Observations of transiting exoplanets have begun to uncover this three-dimensional nature, with JWST measuring their dayside atmosphere structure with eclipse mapping and exploring spectroscopic asymmetries in the limbs of planets during transit. items.title: Extinction by non-spherical particles with the Nanoparticle Transition Matrix Code: perspectives for interstellar medium and exoplanetary atmospheres
items.license: arXiv API terms; metadata CC0
items.abstract: The Transition Matrix formalism (T-matrix) offers an optimal solution to the problem of radiation scattering and absorption by particles characterized by a high degree of chemical and structural complexity. However, its application to particle models composed by large numbers of constituents has been classically limited by the substantial computational burden of the method. As a consequence, the investigation of light scattering and absorption processes, in cases where particle asymmetry and non-homogeneity play an important role, typically need to rely on simplifying assumptions which affect the correct interpretation of transmission spectra and extinction curves. This problem has a huge impact on many fields of scientific application. In particular, it has a critical role in astrophysics, because the ability to model highly non homogeneous particles is a fundamental requirement to understand the role of extinction in different phases of the interstellar medium (ISM), as well as to probe the physics of light transmission in planetary atmospheres within the Solar System and beyond. In this work we describe the application of a new implementation of the T-matrix formalism, based on the framework originally developed by Borghese, Denti & Saija and named Nano-particle Transition Matrix code, which leverages the power of modern hardware architectures to reduce the computational costs related to the solution of relevant particle models for the investigation of dust in the ISM and of hot-Jupyter class planets atmospheric aerosols. This new implementation of the T-matrix formalism can handle calculations of increasing complexity with a direct impact in the interpretation of the transmission spectra of transiting exoplanets produced by the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) and of those expected from the Atmospheric Remote-sensing Infrared Exoplanet Large survey (ARIEL).

items.title: Search for High-Energy Neutrinos from Infrared Flares
items.license: arXiv API terms; metadata CC0
items.abstract: IceCube has detected a diffuse flux of high-energy astrophysical neutrinos. While its astrophysical origin is unknown, a significant neutrino emission has been observed from the gamma-ray blazar TXS 0506+056 and the Seyfert galaxy NGC 1068. This suggests accretion by supermassive black holes as one of the candidate mechanisms of the diffuse neutrino flux. Indeed, external studies that made use of IceCube data identified candidate sources, including AT2019dsg, likely a stellar tidal disruption event (TDE), and AT2019fdr, associated with an active galactic nucleus (AGN). An additional study using an optically detected sample of 63 accretion flares revealed another candidate as a potential high-energy neutrino counterpart: AT2019aalc. All of these candidate transients exhibit strong dust echoes, characterized by delayed infrared (IR) emission relative to the initial optical outburst. We look for correlations between the most comprehensive catalog of infrared flares and 10 years of IceCube archival data. We perform a time-dependent stacking analysis testing 393 sources in the Northern Sky against 10 years of through-going tracks. No significant neutrino emission is observed, and we derive upper limits to constrain neutrino emission from this catalog. These limits are subsequently extrapolated to a population-level study. We find that the contribution of IR flares to the IceCube diffuse neutrino flux at 100 TeV is below 2.7% for a spectral index of 2.5.

items.title: Measurement of Born cross sections of $e^+e^-\to pK^{-}\barΣ^{0}$ + c.c. at $\sqrt{s}$ = 3.5-4.9 GeV and partial wave analysis at $\sqrt{s}$ = 3.773 GeV
items.license: arXiv API terms; metadata CC0
items.abstract: Using $e^+e^-$ collision data collected by the BESIII detector at BEPCII corresponding to a total integrated luminosity of 44.6 $\rm fb^{-1}$, we present the first measurement of the Born cross sections for the process $e^+e^-\to pK^{-}\barΣ^{0}$ + c.c. at fifty-six center-of-mass energies between 3.51 and 4.95~GeV. By fitting the dressed cross sections of $e^+e^-\to pK^{-}\barΣ^{0}$ + c.c. with the assumption of a power-law function plus a charmonium(-like) resonance, i.e., $ψ(3770)$, $ψ(4040)$, $ψ(4160)$, $Y(4230)$, $Y(4360)$, $ψ(4415)$, $ψ(4500)$, $Y(4660)$ or $ψ(4710)$, no significant charmonium(-like) state decaying into $pK^{-}\barΣ^{0}$ + c.c. is observed. The product of branching fractions and electronic partial widths including their upper limits at the 90\% confidence level are provided for each decay. In addition, a partial wave analysis of the process $e^+e^-\to pK^{-}\barΣ^{0}$ + c.c. at $\sqrt{s}$ = 3.773 GeV is performed to investigate $N^{*}$, $Λ^{*}$ and $Σ^{*}$ resonances in the $K^{-}\barΣ^{0}$ and $pK^{-}$ invariant mass spectra. Significant contributions are found from the $Λ(1520)$, $Σ(1670)$, $Σ(1915)$, $N(1900)$, $N(2300)$ and $N(2570)$. The masses, widths and production fractions for each component are determined.

items.title: Search for Sub-Solar Mass Binaries in the First and Second Part of LIGO's Fourth Observing Run O4a-O4b
items.license: arXiv API terms; metadata CC0
items.abstract: The observation of sub-solar mass neutron stars and black holes would signify a new class of astrophysical objects since these systems are not expected to form via standard stellar evolution. We present the first sub-solar mass search for binaries consisting of neutron star or black holes that uses the data from both the second part (O4b) and first part (O4a) of the fourth observing run of the Advanced LIGO detectors. The search covers primary masses 0.1 to 2 $M_\odot$ and secondary masses 0.1 to 1 $M_\odot$. Tidal effects up to $7\times10^5$ are accounted for in extremely low-mass neutron stars. No statistically significant candidates are identified. We place a $90\%$ confidence upper limit on the merger rate $\mathcal{R}_{90}$ for sub-solar mass black holes and neutron stars to be $< 5.2\times10^{2}\,\textrm{Gpc}^{-3}\,\textrm{yr}^{-1}$ for a chirp mass of 0.5 $M_\odot$, a factor $2.2 \times$ lower compared to previous O1-O4a searches. We constrain the effective local dark matter fraction to be $\tilde{f}_\textrm{PBH}<0.6\%$ for $M_{\textrm{PBH}}=0.8 \,M_\odot$, approximately $1.5$ factor improvement to previous O1-O4a constraints. Given our model assumptions, our local dark matter fraction constraints are $2-7$ times lower than the OGLE microlensing survey for $M_{\textrm{PBH}}\ge{0.6}~M_\odot$.

items.title: Cryogenic characterisation of the FBK NUV-HD-cryo Silicon Photomultipliers for the DarkSide-20k dark matter experiment
items.license: arXiv API terms; metadata CC0
items.abstract: Liquid Argon Time Projection Chambers (TPCs) are highly promising detectors for dark matter searches due to their uniform response, scalability to large target masses, and compatibility with ultra-low background conditions. The DarkSide-20k (DS-20k) experiment, currently under construction at Istituto Nazionale di Fisica Nucleare (INFN) Laboratori Nazionali del Gran Sasso (LNGS), aims to achieve unprecedented sensitivity to Weakly Interacting Massive Particles (WIMPs), approaching the neutrino fog. At the heart of the detector is a dual-phase TPC filled and surrounded by low-radioactivity argon from underground sources (i.e. Underground Argon (UAr)), functioning both as the WIMP target and detection medium. The experiment employs Fondazione Bruno Kessler (FBK) NUV-HD-cryo Silicon Photomultipliers (SiPMs) as the chosen photon sensors for its optical planes. Key SiPM properties such as dark noise rate, gain and direct crosstalk were measured using specialized test setups at 77 K. The photon detection efficiency (PDE) was measured under vacuum at 77 K over the wavelength range 350-820 nm. Secondary photon emission, which can give rise to external optical crosstalk, was measured under vacuum at 86 K over the wavelength range 550-1020 nm.

items.license: Crossref metadata CC0; abstract as deposited by publisher
items.abstract: Fast radio bursts (FRBs) are millisecond-duration radio transients from extragalactic sources. Their frequency and polarization properties are affected by plasma and magnetic fields along the line of sight to Earth. We report radio observations of FRB 20240304B and near-infrared follow-up to identify its host galaxy. The host is a low-mass, clumpy, star-forming galaxy at redshift 2.148 ± 0.0013, corresponding to 3 billion years after the Big Bang. This FRB occurred during the peak of cosmic star formation and probes ionized gas over approximately 80% of cosmic history. The highly scattered burst emission implies that there is a population of FRBs that are undetected by current surveys.

items.title: Two families of multi-planet systems with distinct architectures and stellar hosts
items.license: Crossref metadata CC0; abstract as deposited by publisher
items.abstract: The rapidly growing census of exoplanets now includes over a thousand multi-planet systems, revealing architectures that span more than four orders of magnitude in mass and five in orbital scale. Explaining the origin of this striking diversity remains a central challenge for planet formation theory, compounded by observational biases that limit access to Solar System-like regimes. Here we introduce architecture-agnostic metrics to uniformly analyse four independently defined samples of multi-planet systems, uncovering unifying patterns across their diversity. We identify a clear bimodality in system masses, dividing known architectures into two distinct families. The lower-mass family, predominantly hosted by subsolar-to-solar stars, exhibits tightly packed configurations with mass distributions consistent with the ‘peas-in-a-pod’ pattern and modal dynamical excitation comparable with that of the Solar System. By contrast, the high-mass family forms in metal-rich environments around solar-to-supersolar stars, displays gravitationally compact architectures and is an order of magnitude dynamically hotter than both the Solar System and the lower-mass counterparts. Their high level of dynamical excitation points to violent evolutionary pathways driven by global instabilities and planet–planet scattering. Together, these results show that the architectures of planetary systems are born from the combined influence of formation processes and host star properties. Signatures of these roots are preserved across the post-formation dynamical evolution that reshaped most known multi-planet systems.

items.title: Time-Dependent Wave-Packet Approach to Reactions for Quantum Computation
items.license: Crossref metadata CC0; abstract as deposited by publisher
items.abstract: We describe a method for obtaining the scattering matrix for nuclear or chemical reactions on a finite lattice. Aside from the preparation of the initial and final states as wave packets, the only other operation required is unitary time evolution, making this approach ideal for simulations on quantum hardware. The central quantity is a time-dependent overlap between incoming and outgoing wave packets whose Fourier transform corresponds to the scattering matrix at fixed energy, from which one can calculate elastic and inelastic cross sections for reactions involving two interacting clusters. Working in Cartesian coordinates enables an efficient encoding of the problem on quantum hardware via the first quantization mapping, with favorable qubit scaling for describing asymptotic scattering states. Within this framework, we describe a quantum algorithm for probing the scattering amplitude through different angles, including the forward direction, which provides access to the total cross section via the optical theorem. We demonstrate our methods through a series of numerical examples, for both elastic and inelastic processes, comparing against exact calculations. The techniques we describe can more readily be extended to a large number of constituent particles than other existing approaches, once fault-tolerant quantum hardware becomes available.

items.title: Physics of Local Optimization in Complex Disordered Systems
items.license: Crossref metadata CC0; abstract as deposited by publisher
items.abstract: Limited resources motivate decomposing large-scale problems into smaller, “local” subsystems and stitching together the so-found solutions. We explore the physics underlying this approach and discuss the concept of “local hardness,” i.e., the complexity of predicting local properties of the solution from local information, for the ground-state problem of both P- and NP-hard spin glasses and related frustrated spin systems. Depending on the model considered, we observe varying scaling behaviors in how errors associated with local predictions decay as a function of the size of the solved subsystem. These errors are intimately connected to global critical threshold instabilities, characterized by gapless, avalanchelike excitations that follow scale-invariant size distributions. Away from criticality, local solvers quickly achieve high accuracy, aligning closely with the results of the computationally much more expensive global minimization. We leverage these findings to introduce a heuristic contraction-based algorithm for globally studying spin-glass ground states. The local solvers further display sharp imprints of the phase transition from the spin-glass to the ferromagnetic phase as the distribution of spin-glass couplings is shifted, as well as characteristic differences for the infinite-range model, implying the existence of specific classes of local hardness. Our findings shed light on how nature may operate solely through local actions at her disposal.

items.title: A low-cost compact muon detector for millikelvin operation
items.license: arXiv API terms; metadata CC0
items.abstract: Ionizing radiation produces correlated errors in superconducting qubits, posing some challenges to quantum error correction. In addition, it causes background events in other superconducting cryogenic devices, such as kinetic inductance detectors and superconducting nanowire single-photon detectors. Cosmic muons are a component of this background that can only be partly shielded against at ground level, but can be tagged by an independent detector inside the cryostat, so that the affected data can be vetoed, or the muon tags incorporated into error correction. We present a low-cost, compact muon detector consisting of two plastic scintillator modules, each read out by a silicon photomultiplier (SiPM), operated in coincidence. We characterize the SiPMs from room temperature down to 10 mK, including the breakdown and upper-limit voltages that define the operating bias range. Operated as a muon counter, the detector measures a coincidence rate that, as expected, is independent of temperature within uncertainties and agrees with analytical and Monte Carlo predictions. Below approximately 8 K, each muon event produces two pulses, one narrow and one broad, an effect that, to our knowledge, has not been reported before. Coincidences with an independent muon detector outside the cryostat confirm that muons are still counted reliably in this regime. By studying the appearance of double pulses as a function of temperature and magnetic field up to 4.5 T, we find a behavior consistent with the phase diagram of a type-II superconductor. This links the double pulses to a superconducting material in the SiPM, likely an adhesion layer or diffusion barrier introduced during manufacturing. The mechanism by which the superconducting state produces the second pulse is not yet understood.

items.title: Asymmetric enzymatic hydrophosphorylation through O <sub>2</sub> activation
items.license: Crossref metadata CC0; abstract as deposited by publisher
items.abstract: Enzymatic carbon-phosphorus bond formation is extremely rare in nature, limiting biocatalytic access to phosphorus-containing compounds that are widely used in pharmaceuticals and agrochemicals. Here, we report an asymmetric enzymatic hydrophosphorylation through oxygen activation using a repurposed flavin-dependent enzyme. Mechanistic studies revealed that reactive oxygen species are converted into productive phosphorus-centered radicals, followed by radical addition and enzymatic hydrogen atom transfer, achieving high enantioselectivity. The enzyme accommodates diverse phosphorus-hydrogen donors that pose challenges to chemical catalysis, enabling the biosynthesis of valuable phosphorus-containing scaffolds. This work expands the scope of biocatalysis to programmable carbon-phosphorus bond formation and establishes a paradigm for channeling oxygen reactivity in enzymes.

items.title: Advancing mathematics research with AI-driven formal proof search
items.license: Crossref metadata CC0; abstract as deposited by publisher
items.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly excel at mathematics tasks, but their unreliability limits their utility in mathematics research. A mitigation is to use LLMs to generate formal proofs in languages such as Lean, in which the compiler verifies every proof step. We present the first demonstration of this method’s value in solving open problems at scale. We built an artificial intelligence agent for formal proof search that autonomously resolved nine of 353 open Erdős problems, proved 44/492 On-Line Encyclopedia of Integer Sequences conjectures, and is being deployed in combinatorics, optimization, graph theory, algebraic geometry, and quantum optics research. Even a basic agent alternating LLM-based generation with Lean-based verification replicated the Erdős successes. These findings demonstrate the power of formal proof search as an enabler of autonomous mathematical discovery.

items.title: Short-range excitonic correlations and enhanced excitonic susceptibility in 1T-TiSe2
items.license: Crossref metadata CC0; abstract as deposited by publisher
items.abstract: Excitons—bound states of electrons and holes—can spontaneously condense into a quantum coherent ground state. 1 T -TiSe 2 , a layered transition metal dichalcogenide, is a candidate for realizing this phase in a bulk material, but its putative excitonic condensation is accompanied by charge-density-wave formation that obscures signatures of excitonic instability and fluctuations in this structural transition. Here we clarify the mechanism of exciton condensation in quasi-low-dimensional systems by tracking exciton dissociation as a function of photoexcitation fluence and temperature using few-femtosecond broadband extreme-ultraviolet absorption spectroscopy. We find that short-range excitonic fluctuations emerge before long-range-order formation in the ground state. We also observe enhanced excitonic susceptibility, identified by faster exciton dissociation near the phase transition temperature, consistent with excitonic instability in this material. These results provide a framework for understanding other excitonic insulator candidates proposed in quasi-one- or quasi-two-dimensional crystals.

items.title: Sexual dimorphism in epidermal stem cell dynamics
items.license: Crossref metadata CC0; abstract as deposited by publisher
items.abstract: The epidermis is a stratified epithelium comprising proliferative basal cells and differentiated suprabasal cells that are continuously renewed throughout life. Conflicting theories have been proposed regarding the heterogeneity of the basal cell layer, with some studies proposing that all proliferative cells have self-renewal potential during homeostasis 1–5 . Meanwhile, others posit a model in which stem cell differentiation occurs through an intermediate transit-amplifying-like progenitor state with strictly limited proliferative potential 6–10 . Here, to determine the heterogeneity and pattern of cell fate, we performed intravital time-lapse imaging to track the fate of lineage-labelled cells in the skin interfollicular epidermis. Results from quantitative analyses of clonal dynamics support a two-compartment model of epidermal homeostasis, whereby basal cells are organized in a stem cell–transit-amplifying cell hierarchy. Critical to these conclusions was the discovery of sexual dimorphism in epidermal fate, with female mice showing a highly synchronized pattern of cell division, differentiation and delamination that contributes to accelerated wound healing. Single-cell RNA sequencing, transcriptional profiling and clonal analyses of castrated mice revealed that male sex hormones promote stem cell differentiation and delamination. In summary, our study provides insight into the functional identity of the stem cell population and identifies sex-specific differences in the regulation of epidermal stem cells and transit-amplifying cell fate.

items.title: NeuroDETR: Multiscale Discrete Spatiotemporal Tokenization for Asynchronous EEG Event Detection
items.license: arXiv API terms; metadata CC0
items.abstract: Asynchronous EEG event detection supports practical brain-computer interfaces by identifying event classes and temporal boundaries directly from continuous recordings without predefined event boundaries at inference time. The primary challenge lies in extracting event-related patterns embedded in ongoing background activity. To address this, we propose \textbf{NeuroDETR}, a discrete spatiotemporal multiscale framework that combines structured tokenization with event-aware feature refinement. Multiscale temporal codebooks capture brief responses and sustained dynamics, while Spatial-Pyramid VQ hierarchically encodes spatial structure across EEG channels. These complementary representations form a compact event memory for jointly classifying events and estimating their onsets and offsets. Before tokenization, we apply FOCAL, an event-aware sparse attention module that uses predicted event presence to guide temporal feature refinement and spatial aggregation, emphasizing likely event periods while preserving context across the recording. Experiments on eight EEG datasets that span diverse paradigms demonstrate state-of-the-art performance. These findings provide a basis for the development of BCI systems that recognize meaningful neural activity during continuous interaction and monitoring.

items.title: A modern particle-in-cell code for beam-beam simulations of future colliders
items.license: arXiv API terms; metadata CC0
items.abstract: A key challenge in the design of next-generation colliders is predicting the effects of beam-beam interactions and using these predictions to optimize machine performance. Beam-beam interactions are characterized by strong focusing forces, radiative effects, and the generation of background particles. While analytical formulas provide insight into the dynamics of beam-beam interactions, these nonlinear, coupled effects are most accurately described with numerical methods. In this paper, we introduce the open-source particle-in-cell code WarpX as a modern tool for modeling the interaction point in future lepton colliders. WarpX provides high-performance execution on distributed GPU architectures within an open-source and actively maintained code base. We present convergence scans and benchmarks against the established beam-beam codes GUINEA-PIG (v1.2.2) and CAIN (v2.42) for luminosity spectra, photon emission, and secondary-particle production under a wide range of beam parameters corresponding to different collider concepts. Our results show that WarpX (v26.09) reproduces the benchmark beam-beam observables while enabling GPU-portable, extensible simulations. These results establish WarpX as a scalable platform for high-fidelity beam-beam modeling in future collider studies.

items.title: Scaling Discovery Requires Forgetting
items.license: arXiv API terms; metadata CC0
items.abstract: Automated research with LLM agents has shown promising results in various domains. Through iterative refinement and scored verifiers, LLM agents are capable of discovering new ideas. There are different ways to scale automated research: let one agent iterate for longer, run several agents in parallel, or further let the parallel agents communicate and build on one another's candidates. However, we find that all three strategies eventually plateau as the agents accumulate history. Each agent becomes anchored to its own past attempts, making fewer and smaller edits. Beyond this point, additional budget brings little further improvement. In this paper, we show that the key to scaling discovery further is to forget. Periodically discarding the search state, including every agent's session and the candidate history, and restarting from the best candidate found so far, unblocks the search and pushes the same budget further. We implement forgetting in a team of agents with communication and evaluate it on four tasks spanning heuristic programming, kernel optimization and model training. The results show up to 15% improvement compared to parallel agents, and up to 39% compared to a single agent. Our results suggest that, for open-ended discovery, what an agent is allowed to remember matters as much as how much compute it is given.

items.title: Graph-Enhanced Disease Trajectory Discovery and Temporal Endpoint Forecasting from Longitudinal Electronic Health Records
items.license: arXiv API terms; metadata CC0
items.abstract: Longitudinal electronic health records (EHRs) can reveal disease-progression structure, while useful forecasting requires leakage-controlled discovery, censor-aware outcomes, and inspectable trajectory evidence. We developed a graph-enhanced framework in MIMIC-IV v3.1 that splits patients before graph construction, learns train-only consecutive-admission transitions, and freezes endpoint-specific branching-motif policies selected on validation data. The final catalog contained 99,527 motifs, and a time-aware Transformer retrieved at most 24 patient-compatible motifs per endpoint through endpoint-specific cross-attention. Across five training seeds, micro-AUPRC increased from 0.9330 to 0.9357, while event-time MAE decreased from 676.9 to 657.7 days (reduction 19.2 days; 95% paired patient-cluster bootstrap CI, 13.8-24.8). Timing effects were heterogeneous: MAE worsened for events within 730 days but improved by 58.9 days for events occurring after 730 days. In an exploratory internal temporal split, branch conditioning reduced conditional event-time MAE by 26.9 days (95% CI, 23.0-30.8) without evidence of better micro-AUPRC. Corrected survival evaluation over the supported 0-2,555-day interval did not establish macro C-index or integrated Brier score superiority over a matched history-only discrete-hazard model. A directed, degree-matched GNN repair substantially improved unseen-edge discovery, yet replacing GNN-derived scores within fixed motif identities did not improve downstream forecasting. These results position branching motifs as structured trajectory context whose main value is long-range timing support rather than uniformly stronger endpoint discrimination, survival prediction, or causal explanation.

items.title: Quantifying privacy risks in foundation model representations of brain MRI
items.license: arXiv API terms; metadata CC0
items.abstract: Pretrained representations are increasingly used to share and reuse information from medical images without exposing the original scans, but it is unclear how much patient-specific information these representations retain. We investigate this question for brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) by evaluating five frozen pretrained encoders spanning different architectures, pretraining objectives, and training domains on two longitudinal T1-weighted datasets, OASIS-2 and MIRIAD. Under an attacker model with access to released embeddings, the corresponding public encoder, and auxiliary MRI scans, we evaluate patient linkage and sensitive-attribute inference. Across the evaluated representations, we observe substantial subject-specific information: rank-1 patient linkage reaches up to 99\% on MIRIAD and exceeds 90\% on OASIS-2 for the highest-risk representation, despite the absence of an identification objective during encoder training. We further show that the released embeddings retain information about a demographic attribute, with recorded-sex prediction reaching balanced accuracy of 90.9\% on OASIS-2 and 95.5\% on MIRIAD. Overall, our results demonstrate that replacing raw brain MRI with learned embeddings does not, by itself, eliminate patient-linkage or attribute-inference risk, and is therefore insufficient on its own to establish anonymity.

items.title: Oxytocin receptor signaling in the dorsal lateral septum is essential for social transmission of food preference in mice
items.license: CC BY 4.0
items.abstract: by Hanyu Fu, Zhiqiu Liu, Jingwei Zhou, Luyao Zhang, Cai Liu, Dewei Tang, Shuangshuang Zhang, Anan Li, Dejuan Wang Social learning is a fundamental adaptive strategy that critically shapes decision-making and feeding behaviors. Through the social transmission of food preference (STFP), animals acquire information about food safety via social interactions, forming a food-odor memory that overrides innate preferences and guides subsequent food preferences. However, the neural mechanisms through which social cues durably influence feeding preferences remain unclear. Here, we identify the lateral septum (LS) as a key node in STFP. We show that LS neuronal activity increases following social learning and reliably distinguishes between socially cued and uncued foods. Chemogenetic inhibition of the dorsal LS (dLS), but not the ventral LS (vLS), abolishes STFP-driven food preference, revealing subregional specificity within the LS. Furthermore, oxytocin receptor (OXTR) signaling within the dLS is required for STFP in mice, where it enhances neuronal excitability through PLC pathway activation. Together, our results reveal a subregion-specific circuit mechanism through which the dLS integrates social information with feeding motivation, and highlight oxytocinergic modulation as a key mediator of socially guided food preferences.

items.title: High-capacity associative memory in a quantum-optical spin glass
items.license: Crossref metadata CC0; abstract as deposited by publisher
items.abstract: The Hopfield neural network stores memories using all-to-all-coupled spins and recalls those memories through equilibrium dynamics. Storing too many hampers recall because frustration causes an exponential number of spurious patterns to arise as the network becomes a spin glass. Despite this, we show that memory recall can be restored, and even enhanced, under quantum-optical nonequilibrium dynamics that convert spurious patterns into reliable memories. We experimentally observe associative memory with high storage capacity in a driven-dissipative spin glass made of atoms and photons. The capacity surpasses that of the Hopfield model under Hebbian learning by up to sevenfold in a 16-spin network. Atomic motion boosts capacity by dynamically modifying connectivity akin to short-term synaptic plasticity in neural networks, realizing a precursor to learning in a quantum-optical system.

items.title: Volatile eutectics to tailor crystallization for perovskite optoelectronics
items.license: Crossref metadata CC0; abstract as deposited by publisher
items.abstract: Improvements to the radiative efficiency of halide perovskite thin films are necessary to approach fundamental solar cell performance limits. We tailored perovskite crystallization by leveraging the eutectic interaction between zinc bromide and methylammonium chloride additives. The resulting films had high photoluminescence quantum yield and charge carrier decay times and low surface recombination velocity. Nanoprobe x-ray microscopy revealed local melting of the eutectic at grain boundaries during annealing that reduced intragranular structural defect density. Annealing also homogenized the halide distribution and caused zinc segregation to grain boundaries. Solar cells fabricated with the volatile eutectic reached 26.5% power conversion efficiency (PCE, certified 25.9%), and perovskite minimodules (areas more than 15 square centimeters) had 23.9% PCE. Small-area cells with a poly[bis(4-phenyl)(2,4,6-trimethylphenyl)amine] hole transporter retained 85.8% of their initial 24.1% PCE after 1400 hours of continuous operation at 85°C. Furthermore, this approach enables 26.1% external quantum efficiency as light-emitting diodes.

items.title: Golgi-derived vesicles containing PI(3,4)P <sub>2</sub> drive mitochondrial fusion
items.license: Crossref metadata CC0; abstract as deposited by publisher
items.abstract: Mitochondria are dynamic organelles that remodel their shape to regulate cell fate. Mitochondrial division involves interactions with the endoplasmic reticulum (ER), lysosomes, and trans-Golgi network–derived vesicles to facilitate membrane scission. How interorganelle contacts regulate mitochondrial membrane fusion remains largely unknown. Here, we identified a role for Golgi-derived vesicles enriched in phosphatidylinositol 3,4-bisphosphate [PI(3,4)P 2 ] in regulating mitochondrial fusion. We found that these vesicles were recruited to ER- and mitofusin-marked fusion sites. Accordingly, loss of class II PI3-kinase isoforms α and β (PI3K-C2α and PI3K-C2β), which generate PI(3,4)P 2 , led to mitochondrial fragmentation resulting from impaired fusion. Furthermore, cardiomyocyte-specific PI3K-C2α and PI3K-C2β double-deletion mice exhibited mitochondrial fragmentation and heart failure. Thus, subpopulations of Golgi-derived vesicles carrying different phosphoinositides control mitochondrial membrane remodeling and homeostasis.

items.license: CC BY 4.0 (ESA/Webb press releases and images, unless stated otherwise)
items.abstract: First discovered in 2007, fast radio bursts are enigmatic, millisecond-long flashes of radio emission from the distant Universe. Their origin remains uncertain, particularly since most are seen once and never again. Astronomers using the NASA/ESA/CSA James Webb Space Telescope have pinpointed the host galaxy of the most distant fast radio burst (FRB) seen to date. Their finding has implications for what kind of energetic event creates these bursts.

items.title: The 42 problem in AI-assisted research
items.license: CC BY 4.0
items.abstract: Large language models are very good at providing concise answers. But if we only see the answer without knowing the original question or the context behind it, that answer may not be very useful. The important issue is not simply how much information an AI summary removes but whether we can still recover the missing context. Thus, AI literature tools should also report how much information was removed and how recoverable their omissions are.

items.title: Deep learning-based virtual perturbation reveals increasing heterogeneity of gene regulatory responses with aging
items.license: arXiv API terms; metadata CC0
items.abstract: A central hypothesis in aging biology proposes that the gradual accumulation of stochastic molecular damage drives transcriptional deregulation (TD), ultimately leading to functional decline. However, existing single-cell analyses largely rely on static expression measurements and provide limited resolution of how regulatory responses change at the level of individual cells. Here, we leverage DKO, a deep learning framework that predicts cell-specific virtual gene perturbation effects from unperturbed transcriptomes, capturing cell-to-cell differences in regulatory context without requiring a reconstructed gene regulatory network or matched perturbation data. Applying DKO to single-cell transcriptomic datasets from humans, mice, Drosophila, and C. elegans revealed that the transcriptional consequences of perturbing the same gene became increasingly heterogeneous across cells with age, indicating that gene regulatory responses become less consistent and more dependent on cellular context. Furthermore, we find that cells with higher somatic mutation burdens have greater knockout-response variability, linking accumulated molecular damage to regulatory inconsistency. Within the same cellular populations, higher impact variability was also associated with higher senescence scores, linking transcriptional dysregulation to senescence-associated states. Our findings identify a progressive loss of regulatory robustness at both the gene and cell levels as a conserved feature of aging, linking stochastic molecular damage to increasing heterogeneity in cellular regulatory responses.

items.title: Quantum Walks on Arbitrary Spatial Networks with Rydberg Atoms
items.license: CC BY 4.0 (stated on each paper page)
items.abstract: Quantum 10, 2235 (2026). https://doi.org/10.22331/q-2026-10-13-2235 Rydberg atoms provide a highly promising platform for quantum computation, leveraging their strong tunable interactions to encode and manipulate information in the electronic states of individual atoms. Key advantages of Rydberg atoms include scalability, reconfigurable connectivity, and native multi-qubit gates, making them particularly well-suited for addressing complex network problems. These problems can often be framed as graph-based tasks, which can be efficiently addressed using quantum walks. In this work, we propose a general implementation of staggered quantum walks with Rydberg atoms, with a particular focus on spatial networks. We also present an efficient algorithm for constructing the tessellations required for the staggered quantum walk. Finally, we demonstrate that our proposal achieves performance consistent with a quadratic speedup in spatial search algorithms.

items.title: Forecasting of infectious disease epidemics in sexual networks using attenuated renewal processes
items.license: CC BY 4.0
items.abstract: by William D. Green, Christopher E. Overton, Thomas Ward, Ciara V. McCarthy, Sebastian Funk Forecasting emerging infectious disease outbreaks is particularly challenging for sexual networks of men who have sex with men (MSM), where transmission can be shaped by heterogeneous and overdispersed contact structures, mixing assortativity, and both one-time and recurrent partnerships. Using stochastic epidemic simulations on synthetic MSM networks and empirical mpox case data from major cities, we systematically evaluated five classes of short-term forecasting models, from random walk approaches to semi-mechanistic attenuated renewal processes. Model performance was assessed using the continuous ranked probability score (CRPS). Across both simulated and empirical epidemics in heterogeneous networks, renewal models attenuated by a reverse-sigmoid curve, to account for early depletion of highly-connected nodes, consistently outperformed alternatives, achieving more balanced and reliable forecasts. Our findings suggest a practical approach for robust forecasting in highly overdispersed networks, where distinguishing network effects from other factors remains challenging and usually requires additional data.

items.title: Deficiency of placental GDF15 causes fetal growth restriction by inhibiting fetal hepatic STAT3-IGF2 axis
items.license: CC BY 4.0
items.abstract: by Xiao Peng Liu, Xiao Zhang, Chun Xia Cai, Miao Miao Qin, Xiang Kai Leng, Jia Hao Chen, Yi Fan Han, Jun Ying Xiao, Jia He Huang, Jiang Wei Wu Fetal growth restriction (FGR) is a major cause of perinatal morbidity and mortality, yet its underlying mechanism remains elusive. Here, we show that growth differentiation factor 15 (GDF15) levels are significantly reduced in the placenta and fetal circulation in mouse and pig FGR models and correlate positively with fetal weight. Placenta-specific GDF15 deficiency causes FGR, while placenta-specific Gdf15 mRNA delivery through targeted lipid nanoparticle (LNP) effectively alleviates FGR. Mechanistically, placental GDF15 is a major contributor to the fetal circulating GDF15 pool and enters the fetal compartment, where it activates the hepatic STAT3 signaling pathway to stimulate IGF2 production during pregnancy. Placental GDF15 deficiency decreases hepatic STAT3 phosphorylation and IGF2 levels in fetuses. Inhibition of STAT3 in primary mouse fetal hepatocytes blocks GDF15-induced IGF2 upregulation. Placenta-specific Gdf15 mRNA-LNP administration rescues the decreased hepatic p-STAT3 and IGF2 levels in FGR fetuses. Collectively, our findings identify a placenta-fetal liver metabolic axis where placental GDF15 promotes fetal growth by activating the fetal hepatic STAT3-IGF2 pathway, revealing a potential therapeutic target for FGR.

items.license: CC BY 4.0
items.abstract: by James Matthew Ragle, Murugesan Pooranachithra, Guinevere E. Ashley, Emma Cadena, Batia Blank, Katelyn Kang, Cincy Chen, Aditree R. Bhowmick, Soraya H. Mercado, Tabatha E. Wells, John C. Clancy, Andrew D. Chisholm, Jordan D. Ward Barrier epithelia are shielded from the external environment by their apical extracellular matrices (aECMs). The molecular complexity of aECMs has challenged understanding of their organization in vivo. To define the molecular architecture of a model aECM we generated a toolkit of 105 fluorescently tagged aECM components using gene editing in C. elegans , focusing on proteins secreted by the epidermis to form the collagen-rich cuticle. We developed efficient pipelines for modular protein tagging and rapid fluorophore swapping. Most tagged collagens were functional and exhibited exquisitely specific patterning across stages, cell types, and matrix substructures. We define multiple reference markers for key substructures including the little-understood cortical layer, as well as the helical crossed fiber arrays that function as a hydrostatic skeleton to maintain organismal shape. We further tagged 30 members of key aECM protein classes including proteases, protease inhibitors, and lipid transporters. Our standardized markers will allow dissection of the mechanistic basis of aECM spatiotemporal patterning in vivo.

items.title: Multidimensional analysis of social discourse on Twitter (X) around Venezuelan migration in Colombia
items.license: CC BY 4.0 (verified on article pages; occasional CC0)
items.abstract: by Joseph Martínez, Melissa Miller-Felton, Jose J. Padilla, Erika Frydenlund, Katherine Palacio Colombia has become the principal host of Venezuelan migrants in Latin America, prompting a complex mix of solidarity, anxiety, and discrimination. This study offers a multidimensional analysis of Twitter (now X) discourse on Venezuelan migration in Colombia between 2014 and 2022, using natural language processing, geolocation inference, sentiment analysis, and manual annotation of derogatory terms. Drawing from 7.4 million posts, we examine how online discourse evolves across time, space, and language. While negative sentiment is pronounced in original tweets during periods of political and social unrest, our findings highlight that users tend to amplify neutral and positive messages—over 67% of retweets fall into these categories—suggesting an informal counterbalance to polarized discourse. Additionally, the analysis of the derogatory terms veneco and veneca reveals significant gendered patterns: the feminine form veneca appears more frequently in negative contexts, pointing to the gendered dimensions of xenophobic language. These results underscore the dual function of social media as a site of both stigmatization and resistance, offering insights into the emotional and cultural dimensions of migration discourse in Colombia’s digital public sphere.

items.license: CC BY 4.0 (verified on article pages; occasional CC0)
items.abstract: by Xintian Wen, Yanjin Huang To address the lack of a unified quantitative index for the ecological risk assessment of selenium (Se) in soils, the toxicity coefficient of Se was first determined based on Håkanson’s principles, and the spatial distribution and potential ecological risk of Se in surface soils across China were systematically evaluated. The results showed that the toxicity coefficient of Se was determined as 2. Based on the corrected background reference value, approximately 69.9% of the sampling sites were classified as low to moderate ecological risk, 24.4% as considerable risk, and 5.7% as high or very high risk. The elevated risk sites were predominantly confined to localized areas underlain by Se-rich strata, such as Enshi in Hubei Province and Ziyang in Shaanxi Province. A substantial consistency was observed between the potential ecological risk factor (Eri) and the geoaccumulation index (Igeo), with a quadratic weighted Kappa coefficient ( κ w ) of 0.729, indicating that the two classification systems yield comparable results in terms of risk ranking. This study provides a preliminary screening benchmark for identifying areas that warrant further site-specific investigation.

items.title: SPIRE: Spin-Resolved Particle-in-Cell with Radiative Corrections for Extreme Laser--Plasma Interactions
items.license: arXiv API terms; metadata CC0
items.abstract: We present SPIRE, a spin- and photon-polarization-resolved particle-in-cell (PIC) code for self-consistent simulations of laser-plasma interactions in the strong-field quantum electrodynamics (QED) regime. The classical PIC framework combines a Yee-grid finite-difference time-domain Maxwell solver, a relativistic Boris particle pusher, shape-function particle-grid interpolation, Esirkepov charge-conserving current deposition, laser boundary injection, and a relativistic moving window in one, two, and three spatial dimensions. A vectorial Laguerre-Gaussian laser injector based on an angular-spectrum formulation supports tightly focused, nonparaxial optical orbital-angular-momentum modes. The strong-field QED module treats nonlinear Compton scattering and nonlinear Breit-Wheeler pair production as stochastic processes using spin- and polarization-resolved probabilities in the local constant-field approximation. Electron and positron spin evolution includes stochastic transitions, no-emission corrections, and Thomas-Bargmann-Michel-Telegdi precession with a field-dependent anomalous magnetic moment. Photon polarization is represented by the Stokes vector and evolves through nonlinear Compton scattering, pair production, vacuum birefringence, and vacuum dichroism. The implementation is verified with one-, two-, and three-dimensional benchmarks. Classical PIC results are cross-checked against SMILEI, and the spin- and polarization-resolved QED modules reproduce published results for polarized electron generation, vacuum birefringence and dichroism, and dense polarized positron production. These benchmarks verify the coupled classical PIC, strong-field QED, spin, and photon-polarization modules implemented in SPIRE.

items.title: FHiVI$^{2}$: A Fast High-Voltage approach for Ionisation Improvement in the context of plasma-assisted magnetron sputtering
items.license: arXiv API terms; metadata CC0
items.abstract: Ionisation control remains a key challenge in plasma-assisted processes and more particularly in magnetron sputtering. In this context, the former directly governs species transport and thin-film properties. Although HiPIMS substantially enhances the ionisation rate of sputtered species, its performance remains constrained by the coupling between sputtering and ionisation, which limits discharge tunability. Here, we introduce Fast High Voltage for Ionisation Improvement (FHiVI$^{2}$), a new transient electrical regime designed to improve the ionisation rate without requiring additional elements. By applying an ad hoc very short, high-voltage pulse during plasma sputtering processes, FHiVI$^{2}$ regime is expected to induce a strongly anisotropic electric-field burst intended to enhance sputtered metallic species ionisation while limiting back-attraction losses and sputtering. To assess the ionising potential of this regime, optical emission spectroscopy together with mass spectrometry were carried out. More particularly, mass spectrometry measurements show an improvement of the ionisation rate by a factor of 2.7 compared with the HiPIMS regime, for an applied voltage of 2 kV which correspond to an additional mean power of only 1.2 W, using a 2-inch tungsten target. These findings suggest that FHiVI$^{2}$ provides a flexible route towards improved ionisation control in magnetron sputtering and opens new perspectives for plasma-assisted processes.

items.title: Three-dimensional imaging of isolated membrane-protein complexes in vacuo with an X-ray laser
items.license: arXiv API terms; metadata CC0
items.abstract: The prospect of imaging single biomolecules, viruses and cells with intense, ultrashort X-ray pulses has driven the development of X-ray free-electron lasers (XFELs). However, the weak scattering from small particles is easily swamped by background from residual gas, which has so far limited applications to strongly scattering targets such as viruses, cell organelles and cells. Here we report a three-dimensional (3D) reconstruction of an isolated 1-MDa membrane-protein complex, photosystem I (PS I), from single-particle diffraction data. PS I trimers were aerosolised by charge-reduction electrospray ionisation and injected into the European XFEL beam, with partial helium gas exchange reducing background scattering by 80%. From 32 788 diffraction patterns of single trimers in random orientations, we reconstructed the 3D electron density to a resolution of 3.8 nm, limited by the detector geometry. The disc-shaped density, about 22 nm across and 10 nm thick, matches the size of a PS I trimer in a detergent micelle and is consistent with the compaction predicted by molecular dynamics simulations of the complex in vacuo and observed in native mass spectrometry. These results show that membrane-protein complexes can be imaged in vacuo with X-ray lasers, an important step towards ultrafast diffractive imaging of single macromolecules.

items.title: Starvation transforms signal encoding in C. elegans thermoresponsive neurons and suppresses heat avoidance via bidirectional glutamatergic and peptidergic signaling
items.license: CC BY 4.0
items.abstract: Animals must continuously adapt their behavioral outputs in response to changes in internal state, including nutritional state. Here, we show that starvation induces a profound and progressive suppression of thermonociceptive behavior in Caenorhabditis elegans . During early food deprivation (1 hr without food), the thermoresponsive AWC sensory neurons mediate robust heat-evoked reversals over a broad range of stimulus intensities via glutamate and FLP-6 neuropeptide signaling, each covering distinct heat intensity ranges. After 6 hr of food deprivation (prolonged starvation), heat-evoked reversal responses are nearly abolished, independently of external food odor cues. Starvation shifts the distribution of AWC heat-evoked calcium response polarity, from mostly excitatory responses to a heterogeneous pattern combining excitatory and inhibitory activities. This switch relies on ASI neurons, proposed to sense internal state. INS-32 and NLP-18 neuropeptide signals from ASI switch from reversal-promoting to reversal-inhibiting effects. In addition, reversal-promoting glutamatergic transmission by AWC is antagonized by glutamatergic transmission from non-AWC neurons that suppress FLP-6-dependent reversals. Our findings define a circuit logic by which gating of nociceptive responsiveness by internal nutritional state is linked to dynamic modulation of sensory neuron activity patterns

items.title: Punctuated mutagenesis promotes multi-step evolutionary adaptation in human cancers
items.license: CC BY 4.0
items.abstract: The rate of acquisition of genomic changes in cancer has been the topic of much discussion, with several recent investigations finding evidence of punctuated evolution instead of gradual accumulation of such changes. items.title: The structural context of mutations in proteins predicts their effect on antibiotic resistance
items.license: CC BY 4.0
items.abstract: In Mycobacterium tuberculosis , a prevalent and deadly pathogen, resistance to antibiotics evolves primarily through non-synonymous mutations in proteins. Sequence-based analyses can uncover the genetic basis of antibiotic resistance, but these methods focus on primary sequence and often neglect other biological signals, such as protein structural information. items.title: Composable logical gate error in approximate quantum error correction: reexamining gate implementations in Gottesman-Kitaev-Preskill codes
items.license: CC BY 4.0 (stated on each paper page)
items.abstract: Quantum 10, 2230 (2026). https://doi.org/10.22331/q-2026-10-08-2230 Quantifying the accuracy of logical gates is paramount in approximate error correction, where perfect implementations are often unachievable with the available set of physical operations. To this end, we introduce a single scalar quantity we call the (composable) logical gate error. It captures both the deviation of the logical action from the desired target gate as well as leakage out of the code space. items.title: Approach to optimal quantum transport via states over time

items.abstract: Quantum 10, 2236 (2026). https://doi.org/10.22331/q-2026-10-14-2236 We approach the problem of constructing a quantum analogue of the immensely fruitful classical transport cost theory of Monge from a new angle. Going back to the original motivations, by which the transport is a bilinear function of a mass distribution (without loss of generality a probability density) and a transport plan (a stochastic kernel), we explore the quantum version where the mass distribution is generalised to a density matrix, and the transport plan to a completely positive and trace preserving map. These two data are naturally integrated into their Jordan product, which is called state over time (“stote''), and the transport cost is postulated to be a linear function of it. We explore the properties of this transport cost, as well as the optimal transport cost between two given states (simply the minimum cost over all suitable transport plans). After that, we analyse in considerable detail the case of unitary invariant cost, for which we can calculate many costs analytically. These findings suggest that our quantum transport cost is qualitatively different from Monge's classical transport.

items.title: Salmonids elicit an acute behavioral response to heterothermal environments
items.license: CC BY 4.0
items.abstract: Most fish species are ectothermic and rely on behavioral strategies to control their body temperature in heterothermal environments. Both thermotaxis and thermokinesis have been suggested as important underlying mechanisms. However, to what extent these behaviors allow fish to respond to rapid (timescales of minutes) and strong thermal disturbances, like those caused by anthropogenic water releases into natural freshwater systems, is poorly understood. Here, we quantify this response for a salmonid species with a novel laboratory approach coupled with image-based tracking. We exposed brown trout parr ( Salmo trutta ), acclimated to 12 °C, to rapidly forming cold- and warm-water interfaces with temperatures ranging from 4 to 20 °C. We found that fish actively avoided colder water (≤8 °C) through a rapid response that combined thermotaxis and thermokinesis. In contrast, fish did not avoid warmer water and frequently crossed interfaces having temperature contrasts of up to 8 °C. This study shows that brown trout parr swiftly deploy multiple behavioral strategies to minimize exposure to cold water and take advantage of warm water, illustrating their capability to cope with rapidly occurring thermal alterations.

items.title: Spatial Kernel Restricted Canonical Correlation Analysis: Population Targets, Identifiability, and Stability
items.license: arXiv API terms; metadata CC0
items.abstract: Relating observations of different categories across space requires methods that accommodate distinct sampling locations and spatial dependence. Spatial kernel restricted canonical correlation analysis (skrCCA) uses spatial weights to identify associated feature combinations across data categories. Here, we develop a statistical theory of its covariance form after feature reduction. Conditional on the observed locations and under a mean-zero model, the pairwise association matrices target kernel-weighted averages of cross-covariances. For prespecified directions, we derive the exact null variance under independence between blocks. We establish recovery and stability bounds in two- and multiblock settings under explicit population models, and show that exact cyclic updates have convergent objective values. The variance characterization shows how spatial weighting and within-block dependence jointly determine the effective information available for estimating association. The recovery bounds separate statistical and optimization error, relating stability to population separation and the strength of connections between blocks. These results clarify what fitted spatial association axes estimate and provide conditions under which they can be recovered reliably.

items.abstract: Human African trypanosomiasis (HAT) is a neglected tropical disease transmitted by infected tsetse flies (Glossina spp.) in sub-Saharan Africa. Infected tsetse flies can transmit trypanosomes, including Trypanosoma brucei subspecies that cause HAT in humans, as well as other trypanosome species that cause animal African trypanosomiasis in domestic animals and infect wildlife. Tsetse flies feed on a broad spectrum of hosts, including humans, elephants, buffaloes, rhinos, hippos, turtles, and monitor lizards. To understand how the insects can penetrate such diverse skin types, we detailed the anatomical structures involved in tsetse blood feeding, their mechanical properties, and the forces exerted by the fly during probing. We found that the tsetse fly’s feeding apparatus does not rely on exceptionally unique structures or extraordinary forces. Instead, the tsetse fly has evolved subtle yet highly efficient adaptations, which include a labellum equipped with arrays of small teeth. When combined with a robust retraction movement of the proboscis, these structures create lesions on various types of skin, thus facilitating blood pool feeding on a broad host spectrum.

items.license: CC BY 4.0
items.abstract: Neural circuit assembly relies on the precise regulation of cell-surface receptors that mediate signaling and adhesion. Endocytosis controls receptor activity and availability by internalizing and routing proteins through early endosomes to one of two main pathways: recycling back to the cell-surface or delivery to lysosomes for degradation. Rab GTPases direct receptors into these distinct pathways, but their specific contributions to circuit formation remain opaque. Using clonal analyses with null alleles, we dissected the roles of Rab-mediated trafficking to early, late, and recycling endosomes across multiple stages of circuit assembly in vivo. Our approach revealed that Rab5 and Rab11 regulate extensive and largely distinct developmental events, highlighting the pivotal roles of early endosome sorting and recycling pathways in circuit assembly. As neurons mature, both the spatial distribution and abundance of specific endocytic compartments change to reflect evolving trafficking demands. Our findings underscore how distinct post-endocytic trafficking fates are necessary to build neural circuits.

items.title: Calibrating AlphaFold confidence scores for interface quality
items.license: arXiv API terms; metadata CC0
items.abstract: AlphaFold confidence scores are widely used to rank protein complex predictions and to select subsets of models for downstream applications. Although these scores provide strong discriminatory power for distinguishing prediction quality, their numerical values were never intended to represent the probability that a prediction satisfies a given structural quality criterion. In this work, we calibrate commonly used confidence scores to estimate the probability that a predicted complex exceeds a chosen threshold of DockQ, an established measure of interface quality. On antibody-antigen and general multimer datasets, post-hoc isotonic calibration consistently improves agreement between predicted probabilities and observed DockQ success rates while preserving the underlying score ordering. The calibrated probabilities also provide more accurate estimates of the fraction of selected models expected to pass a given structural quality threshold. Although the mapping is fitted within a given prediction distribution and therefore transfers imperfectly across prediction domains, we show that reliable estimates are recovered from a small number of labeled target-domain samples. Because the calibration is entirely post hoc and requires no underlying AlphaFold model fine-tuning, it provides a straightforward and customizable way to convert existing model quality rankings into calibrated probabilities of passing a chosen structural quality threshold.
